**01**

# **What Space Apps is**

Space Apps is the world’s largest annual hackathon. Over one weekend, teams at hundreds of events around the world use open data from NASA and its Space Agency Partners to build solutions to real problems on Earth and in space. Challenges are written by NASA subject matter experts and span software, hardware, data science, design, and storytelling.

**The 2025 edition, in numbers:**

| Registered participants | 114,094 | Challenges | 18 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Countries & territories | **167** | Space Agency Partners | **14 (17 in 2026\)** |
| Teams | **18,860** | NASA subject matter experts | **124** |
| Projects submitted | **11,511** | Universal Event registrations | **8,025** |
| Local Events | **551** | Navigators | **78** |
| Social mentions reach | **617M** | Global Offers / collaborators | **11 / 19** |

India, Egypt, Brazil, Türkiye, and the United States sent the most registrants in 2025\. For 2026 the partner count rises to seventeen, with Angola, the Korea AeroSpace Administration, Nigeria’s NASRDA, and Senegal’s agency joining for the first time.

Bangladesh has competed since the inception of the NASA Space Apps Challenge in 2012 and has produced global winners four times. In 2026 the country returns with Local Events in cities nationwide, all feeding the same global judging pipeline.

**02**

# **Space Apps Challenge Brief**

The NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 comes to Bangladesh on Friday 13 and Saturday 14 November, across nine cities. Bangladesh runs a day ahead of the 14–15 November global window so the hackathon falls on the local weekend. Any Bangladeshi student can take part — from a city venue where one is confirmed, or virtually from anywhere in the country.

Continuing the legacy, with the Local Leads. Bangladesh has entered Space Apps since the challenge began in 2012, taking four global championships and putting teams into the finalist round again and again. The 2026 edition carries that record forward under the city Local Leads, who run the national edition together: nine cities, one shared calendar, one two-day format, one judging pipeline.

**04**

# **Two registrations, one project**

Bangladesh runs a national pre-registration alongside the global NASA registration. They are separate systems and you need both. Teams lose their place every year by doing only one.

|  | BANGLADESH PRE-REGISTRATION | NASA SPACE APPS REGISTRATION |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Opens** | 25 August 2026 | 26 August 2026 |
| **Where** | The Bangladesh registration form, published by your Local Lead | spaceappschallenge.org |
| **What it gets you** | Your seat at a Bangladesh Local Event, and your place in local judging | Your team page, your challenge, and your entry into global judging |
| **What you submit there** | Your 240-second prescreening video by 1 October, then the local judging cut during the hackathon | Your final project — summary, demo, links, and data used |
| **Skip it and…** | You cannot take part locally or be judged locally | You have no project in the competition at all |

**READ THIS TWICE**

Pre-registering in Bangladesh does not register you with NASA. Whatever happens at your local event, you must register your team and submit your final project on the NASA Space Apps website — that submission is the only thing global judges ever see. The closing date for Bangladesh pre-registration is set by the Local Leads and announced with the form; do not wait for it.

**06**

# **Who should join**

Students, technologists, and citizen scientists. No matter your age, skill level, or professional background, when you take part you join a global community that uses NASA open data to answer today’s most pressing science and space exploration challenges.

The strongest teams are the mixed ones — six developers usually lose to a team with a developer, a designer, a domain researcher, and someone who can tell the story in three minutes. Developers, designers and artists, data scientists, researchers, hardware and robotics engineers, storytellers and filmmakers, entrepreneurs, educators, students of any age, citizen scientists, and anyone curious enough to try.

## **Eligibility**

* Open to all ages, all nationalities, all skill levels.

* Participants under 18 must be registered for the event by a parent or legal guardian, and must be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian at all times during the event.

* Full rules are in the Participant Terms & Conditions at spaceappschallenge.org/legal.

## **Team rules**

* One to six members. Teams may be cross-city.

* One event per participant — your project competes there.

* You may finalise or change your team any time before you submit.

## **What counts as a project**

* Software, hardware, a data product, a model, a game, a design, a film, or an article — all are valid.

* It must use open data from NASA or a Space Agency Partner.

* It must answer one published 2026 challenge.

**NOBODY PAYS**

Participation is free at every event, everywhere. If you are asked to pay money for any part of a NASA Space Apps event, do not pay anything — report it to info@spaceappschallenge.org.

**08**

# **Your three videos**

Bangladesh teams make three videos, not one video cut three ways. Two run to 240 seconds and gate your place locally; the third runs to 30 seconds and is all a NASA judge on the other side of the world will ever see. Budget real time for each — strong projects lose here every year.

| VIDEO | MAXIMUM | MUST CONTAIN | WHERE IT GOES | DEADLINE |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1 · Prescreening** 240 Seconds of Glory Qualification and entry | **240 sec** 4 minutes | Team name Every team member, listed by name Problem and challenge statement Solution approach — concept only | Upload to YouTube, then paste the link into the Google Form | **1 October** 11:59 PM |
| **2 · Local judging** 240 Seconds of Glory Judged at your city event | **240 sec** 4 minutes | Team name Every team member, listed by name Problem and challenge statement Solution, plus a demo of it working State your NASA data usage out loud in the video | Upload to YouTube and paste the link into the Google Form, and upload the file to the Google Drive folder provided | **1 November** 6:30 PM |
| **3 · Global judging** 30 Seconds of Glory The final video | **30 sec** | Team name Every team member, listed by name Problem and challenge statement Solution, plus a demo of it working State your NASA data usage All Space Apps documentation completed alongside it | Upload to YouTube or Vimeo, then paste the link into the Google Form and into your NASA project page | **14 November** 12:00 PM |

**CHECK WITH YOUR LEAD**

Video 2’s 1 November date sits oddly against the run of show in section 02, which puts the 240-second upload at 6:30 PM on Friday 13 November — day one of the hackathon. The time matches exactly, so 1 November may be a carry-over; treat the run of show as the working schedule and confirm with your Local Lead.

Video 3 is solid: the 12:00 PM cut-off on the final day is the long-standing rule for the global nomination video, and your Local Lead needs it before nominations go to NASA.

The prescreening video is due before challenge statements are published on 28 October, so build it from the challenge summaries released on 17 September. Concept only is fine at that stage — that is what the form asks for.

![][image3]

*Adapted from the official NASA Space Apps 240 Seconds of Glory pitch model. Use it for both 240-second videos — video 1 stops at the concept, video 2 fills the third and fourth blocks with the working build.*

## **Prescreening to local judging**

* Video 1 secures your seat, and it can be re-cut right up to the hackathon.

* Video 2 is the same pitch with the demo dropped in and your NASA datasets named on camera.

* Video 2 goes to YouTube and to the Google Drive folder your Local Lead provides.

## **Hard limits on the 240s**

* Under 240 seconds. Over-length videos get cut off, not excused.

* Name every team member — both videos, every time.

* Credit any third-party asset, template, or generated content you used.

![][image4]

*A 30-second beat sheet. The hard rules are NASA’s; the timings are a working suggestion, not a requirement.*

## **Where video 3 goes**

* YouTube or Vimeo, then the link goes into both the Google Form and your NASA project page.

* Test the link in a private window. If a judge cannot open it, your project cannot be judged.

* A seven-slide deck is an accepted NASA alternative to the video — but the video travels better.

## **Do not lose marks on this**

* English subtitles are required on video demos; slide decks must be in English.

* No recognisable names, voices, or faces of anyone under 18\.

* Show the thing working. A slideshow about a thing is not a demo of a thing.

* Finish your Space Apps documentation alongside video 3, not after it.

**09**

# **Be ready before day one**

* **Registered and assigned to an event** — Do it the day registration opens.

* **Under 18? Guardian registered you and is coming** — They must be with you throughout the event.

* **240-second prescreening video uploaded** — YouTube link in the Google Form by 1 October, 11:59 PM.

* **Team confirmed, roles agreed** — Decide who builds, who researches, who presents.

* **NASA Earthdata account created** — Free, and the gateway to most Earth-observation datasets.

* **GitHub repository ready and public** — Judges look at what you actually built.

* **Environment set up and tested** — Install and test before you arrive, not at hour two.

* **Datasets downloaded offline** — Never rely on venue bandwidth for a large download.

* **Laptop, charger, extension cord, power bank** — Sockets run out fast.

* **Slide template and demo script started** — Two hours of prep saves you the last two hours.

* **Sleep, food, and water planned** — It is a two-day sprint, not an all-nighter contest.

**10**

# **Submitting on the NASA site**

Everything global judges see lives on your NASA project page. Nothing else — not your local pitch, not the room you were in, not how hard the weekend was — reaches them. Fill it in properly during the hackathon, not in the last twenty minutes.

## **Step by step**

| 1 | Log in to spaceappschallenge.org. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **2** | Open the Members tab and make sure every team member is listed, with a photo and their role. |
| **3** | Add your team photo. This is the picture that runs beside your name if you win globally. |
| **4** | Go to your challenge category and topic. |
| **5** | Fill in every field below, with links and documentation. |
| **6** | Click Submit. An unsubmitted page is not judged. |

## **What each field must contain**

| FIELD | WHAT GOES IN IT |
| :---- | :---- |
| **High-Level Summary** | Name your project, then summarise it: what you built, who it helps, how it works. Include the link to your 240-second video and your GitHub link here. |
| **Project Demo** | Your 30-second YouTube video, under 30 seconds, built to the beat sheet in section 08\. A seven-slide deck is NASA’s accepted alternative. |
| **Final Project** | The detail behind the build — Figma, GitHub, or other full documentation. |
| **Project Details** | Where you shine. Use pictures, detail, and links across the three blocks below. |
| **GitHub or Drive access** | Whatever you link must be open and public so any judge can evaluate it, with no login or permission request. Test it in a private window before you submit. |
| **Use of AI** | Every AI tool in your solution, named — with the prompts and reasoning behind them, and the data the AI worked on. |
| **NASA data sources used** | List every NASA and partner dataset, then say what you used it for and how. Judges check this against your claims. |
| **References** | Every source, paper, dataset, library, and asset you drew on. |

## **The three Project Details blocks**

* **The why, the what, the how** — How you addressed the challenge, and how you developed the project — listing every dataset you used, in detail.

* **Community involvement** — What you hope to achieve, anything important the reader must know, your highlighted features, and the benefits they bring.

* **Tools and technologies** — Tools, languages, and frameworks used, with credit given generously.

**UNDER-18 RULE**

Recognisable names, voices, and likenesses of people under the age of 18 must not appear in any video or project submission. Plan your demo around this from the start — reshooting on Saturday afternoon is a bad way to spend your last hours.

**11**

# **How you are judged**

There are three passes, and one score sheet runs through all of them. Whether you sit at the mainstage in Dhaka or work from your bedroom in Cumilla, the same five judges score your city’s projects against the same criteria.

![][image5]

## **To be eligible for any award, you must**

* **Answer an official 2026 Space Apps challenge** — One published challenge, clearly named on your project page.

* **Link a public repository** — Code and documentation, openly accessible — test the link.

* **Use NASA open data** — Other data is welcome on top. NASA data is not optional.

* **Keep event code open source** — Anything you build during the weekend stays open.

* **Register and identify every team member** — On the team’s NASA page, with roles.

## **The score sheet**

| \# | CRITERION | POINTS | WHAT IT MEASURES |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | **Impact** | **1–20** | The scale and significance of the problem, and how far the solution reaches. |
| 2 | **Creativity** | **1–20** | Originality of the idea and of the execution. |
| 3 | **Validity** | **1–20** | Scientific soundness, technical feasibility, usability. |
| 4 | **Relevance** | **1–20** | Alignment to the challenge, and how deeply NASA data sits at the core. |
| 5 | **Presentation** | **1–20** | Clarity, structure, storytelling, and reach to a broad audience. |
| 6 | Teamwork | 1–5 | Evidence of genuine collaboration across the team. |
| 7 | User experience | 1–5 | 5 \= anyone can use it. 1 \= it needs significant training. |
| 8 | NASA data usage | 1–5 | 5 \= NASA open data plus other agency or third-party sources, clearly shown. |
| 9 | Challenge category identified | 0 or 1 | A 2026 challenge category is named. |
| 10 | Repository access | 0 or 1 | GitHub or Drive link works and is open to all. |
| 11 | Project page complete | 0 or 1 | The NASA project page is filled in and submitted. |
| — | **Women participation bonus** | **\+5%** | Teams with one or more women members receive 5% on top of the aggregate. |

Criteria 1–5 carry the headline 100 points. Criteria 6–8 add up to 15, and 9–11 add up to 3, for a maximum of 118 before the bonus. The 5% is applied to the aggregate at the end.

## **The anchor scale for criteria 1–5**

| SCORE | BAND | WHAT IT MEANS |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **20** | **Absolutely wow** | The concept is unique. I could not have imagined it, and I don’t think anyone else could either. |
| **10** | **Unique idea** | Idea and implementation are unique, but I have heard of a similar concept somewhere. I have not seen it built. |
| **5** | **Unique implementation** | The idea is already in the public domain, but this implementation is unique. |
| **1** | **Public domain** | Concept, idea, and implementation are all already available publicly. |

## **1 · Impact**

What is the project’s potential for significant impact, in quality and quantity? Does it address a major problem or a minor one? How far does it inspire or help others?

| 20 | Addresses a major global or local challenge with a transformative solution. Clear pathways to scale and sustain across regions or sectors. Inspires adoption by NGOs, policymakers, or startups. Measurable outcomes are plausible — emissions cut, lives saved, education reached. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **10** | A meaningful problem framed innovatively, but needing more work to scale globally. Impact is real but limited to a smaller audience or proof-of-concept. |
| **5** | A moderate or local issue. Useful to a niche audience, harder to scale beyond the team’s own community. |
| **1** | Minimal impact. A minor issue, or little added value beyond what already exists publicly. |

*Judges ask: Who benefits? How many? How measurable is the positive effect?*

## **2 · Creativity**

How original is the approach? Is this a novel concept, or a meaningful improvement on an existing one? Does the creativity distinguish it from conventional methods?

| 20 | A bold, original idea, or a radical new spin on existing work. Makes unexpected connections — cross-disciplinary, cultural, artistic, gamified. Sets a new benchmark. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **10** | Genuine originality and a new perspective, though similar approaches exist. A clear improvement or remix that adds real value. |
| **5** | A widely known concept, but the team shows creativity in execution — design, storytelling, or application. |
| **1** | Conventional, predictable, undistinguished. |

*Judges ask: Does this feel fresh and surprising, or predictable and routine?*

## **3 · Validity**

Is the method grounded in scientific principles? Is it technically feasible? Would it work in the real world, and can an ordinary person use it?

| 20 | Scientifically robust, using validated data and methods. Technically feasible with a working prototype or demo. Usability tested, accessible beyond experts, with clear performance metrics. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **10** | Largely valid but needing more testing. The prototype shows feasibility without stress-testing or broader validation. Some usability work in place. |
| **5** | Partially valid. Methods align with science but are oversimplified. The prototype works under limited conditions; usability is minimal or inconsistent. |
| **1** | Not scientifically credible, technically impractical, or unable to show basic feasibility. |

*Judges ask: Would this work if deployed tomorrow? Is it rigorous and trustworthy?*

## **4 · Relevance**

Does the project fully and directly answer the challenge it was submitted against? Is NASA data a core component of the method, or a superficial addition?

| 20 | Fully aligned with the selected challenge and beyond expectations. NASA data is central and used creatively, not merely cited. Deep understanding of both challenge and dataset, with reproducible, transparent data usage. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **10** | Strong alignment, but NASA data integration is moderate — helpful rather than essential. The challenge is addressed meaningfully, with some aspects underexplored. |
| **5** | Partial relevance. Responds to the challenge loosely. NASA data is referenced but not integral to the solution. |
| **1** | Weak alignment. NASA data is barely used, or irrelevant to the main idea. |

*Judges ask: Is this NASA-data-first, or just NASA-data-added?*

## **5 · Presentation**

How clearly did the team convey the challenge, the method, and why it matters? How well-structured and engaging was the storytelling?

| 20 | Flawless: a clear, structured, compelling narrative with a beginning, middle, and end. Polished visuals and audio, in clear English. Connects emotionally and intellectually. Leaves judges saying, “I get it, and it matters.” |
| :---- | :---- |
| **10** | Very good, with gaps in clarity, pacing, or flow. Visuals engaging but uneven in polish. English is clear and understood. |
| **5** | Adequate but rushed, unclear, or missing key elements. Visuals are good but need polishing; the language repeats itself and could be tightened. |
| **1** | Confusing, incomplete, or poorly executed. Graphics, audio, and video need work, and judges struggle to follow the purpose. |

*Judges ask: Could a global audience understand and remember this in 240 seconds?*

**JUDGING FAIRLY**

Judges are briefed to check themselves for affinity bias — favouring people with similar backgrounds and interests; confirmation bias — favouring what supports their existing beliefs; and the halo effect — letting one positive impression colour everything else. Every team in a region is scored by the same panel of five judges. That is the structural guarantee behind the promise that where you sat does not matter.

**NOTE FOR JUDGES**

At the prescreening pass, projects arrive incomplete — NASA has not published the full challenge statements yet. Score them from that perspective. The one non-negotiable: read the challenge, and check that the presentation actually answers it. That is what relevance is measuring.

**12**

# **Awards and nominations**

## **At your city**

| AWARD | HOW MANY | WHO GETS IT |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Local winners** | Up to 2 | The top-scoring projects at your location, by the score sheet in section 11\. The exact number depends on how many teams finally submitted. |
| **Innovation Space / People’s Choice** | 0 or 1 (optional) | A project that won nothing else but made strikingly creative use of NASA open data, or was simply inspirational. Judges may decline to give it. |
| **Global nomination** | 1 per 10 projects submitted | Counted against the projects on the submission page at the final submission time. Twenty submissions means two nominations; every further ten adds one. |

**FINAL MEANS FINAL**

Local judging is at the discretion of the panel appointed for each location, and the decision is final. Nominations are decided behind closed doors and cannot be appealed — a team that challenges the decision is automatically removed from global nomination.

## **Globally**

NASA experts review nominations from Local Leads worldwide, shortlist roughly thirty Global Finalists, and pick one winner in each category below. They judge from your project page — so keep the description, the video, and the open-source links current right through the judging window. Global winners are featured on the Space Apps website and invited to visit a NASA centre with the Global Organizing Team; travel, meals, and accommodation are the winners’ own responsibility.

| CATEGORY | AWARDED TO |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Best Use of Science** | The solution making the best and most valid use of science or the scientific method. |
| **Best Use of Data** | The solution that best makes space data accessible, or applies it uniquely. |
| **Best Use of Technology** | The solution exemplifying the most innovative use of technology. |
| **Galactic Impact** | The solution with the most potential to improve life on Earth or in the universe. |
| **Best Mission Concept** | The solution with the most plausible concept and design. |
| **Most Inspirational** | The solution that captures our hearts. |
| **Best Storytelling** | The solution that most creatively communicates the potential of open data through storytelling. |
| **Global Connection** | The solution that best connects people around the world through technology. |
| **Art & Technology** | The solution that most effectively combines technical and creative skills. |
| **Local Impact** | The solution demonstrating the greatest potential for local impact. |

Local judges also tick which of these categories they are nominating a project for. That is a yes/no mark, not a score — it does not affect your points.

**13**

# **Why it is worth your weekend**

* **Real data, real stakes** — You work with the same open datasets used by scientists and mission teams, on problems written by the people who study them.

* **A portfolio piece** — A finished, documented, publicly judged project is worth more in an application than any certificate.

* **A global stage** — Bangladeshi teams have won global categories before. The nomination path from your city to NASA judging is short and real.

* **The network** — Mentors, judges, and the people you build with over two days tend to stay in your life far longer than the weekend.

**14**

# **Conduct and support**

* **The standard** — Space Apps aims to be a place where everyone feels they belong, is comfortable being authentic, and is empowered to contribute fully. Discrimination, harassment, and bullying in any form are not tolerated.

* **If you experience or witness it** — Contact your Local Lead, the NASA Space Apps Global Organizing (GO) Team at conduct@spaceappschallenge.org, or both. The GO Team will take appropriate action, which may include warning or expelling offending participants from the event.

* **Accessibility** — If you need step-free access, an interpreter, a quiet space, or anything else to participate fully, contact your Local Lead before the event so it can be arranged.

**15**

# **Questions we get every year**

## **Where do my code and documentation go?**

Push everything to GitHub and give the link: your code, your full documentation, your journey, your project description, your video, your poster, and any other links. Google Drive or OneDrive is accepted instead — but the folder must be set to full public access, and you should test it in a private window before you submit.

## **Can I use someone else’s content?**

No. You may not use copyrighted material, or anything owned by someone else, without their explicit consent. This applies to code, images, audio, footage, and datasets alike.

## **Can I use AI-generated content?**

Yes, with conditions: you need a valid reason for using it, you must explain your prompts, and you must show where your own creative work went. Unexplained generated content is not acceptable, and any tool used to generate content must be named in your description.

## **What about stock content?**

If you intend to win, do everything yourself. Where you genuinely must use royalty-free material, add a disclaimer, credit the source, and give a valid reason for using it.

## **And premium or paid content?**

Allowed, with proper credits, disclaimers, and reasons — provided it supports your solution rather than being it. A purchased website theme is fine when the content on the site is yours; a Figma template is fine when you have customised it. The core must be your own work.

## **Where do I find this year’s challenges?**

At spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges. Set “Show Challenges From” in the top-right corner to “2026 NASA Space Apps Challenges” — the page can default to a previous year, and every year teams build against the wrong list. Summaries land 17 September, full statements 28 October.
